title.en: Essere and avere: 'to be', 'to have', and everyday feelings

summary.en: Master the two core verbs of Italian—including expressions where Italian 'has' what English 'is'.

body.en:
From season 1, episodes 1 and 5.

Almost every introduction at the inn starts with *essere* ('to be'): Chiara announces *Sono* Chiara ('I am Chiara'), and Bruno answers *Io sono* Bruno, *sei in anticipo* ('you are early'). Meanwhile *avere* ('to have') handles both possessions and physical or mental states—Cesare admits *Hai ragione* ('You are right', literally 'You have reason') and sinks onto a chair sighing *Ho le gambe deboli* ('My legs feel weak').

| Person | *essere* ('to be') | *avere* ('to have') |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *io* | *sono* | *ho* |
| *tu* | *sei* | *hai* |
| *lui / lei / Lei* | *è* | *ha* |
| *noi* | *siamo* | *abbiamo* |
| *voi* | *siete* | *avete* |
| *loro* | *sono* | *hanno* |

Notice silent initial `h` in *ho*, *hai*, *ha*, *hanno*: it is never pronounced, yet in writing it distinguishes *ha* ('has') from *a* ('at/to') and *hanno* ('they have') from *anno* ('year'). Remember common *avere* expressions too: *avere ragione* ('be right'), *avere freddo* ('be cold'), *avere caldo* ('be hot'), and *avere paura* ('be afraid').

On replay, compare accented *è* ('is', open /ɛ/) with silent-`h` *hai* and *ho*.
